Abstract: With the continuous expansion of global transportation infrastructure and the increasing frequency of extreme climate events, the risk of instability of soft rock slopes has increased dramatically. The combined effects of complex geological structures and non-stationary hydroclimatic forcing make traditional stability analysis methods and control technologies inadequate and unreliable. Recently, numerous novel approaches for the stability analysis and control of soft rock slopes have emerged. This paper systematically reviews these approaches and their core advances. The mechanical behaviour and degradation mechanisms of soft rocks are reviewed within a coupled multiphysics framework, covering soft rock classification, typical characteristics, transient and time-dependent responses, deformation behaviour and constitutive characterization and parameter evolution. The effects of individual and coupled environmental factors on rock degradation are elucidated. Secondly, stability analysis methods for soft rock slopes are reviewed, incorporating both conventional approaches and their recent advances. The improved methodologies encompass theoretical advances in (1) limit-equilibrium and block-kinematic formulations; (2) numerical modelling across continuum, discontinuum and multiscale frameworks; (3) reliability-based analyses integrating probabilistic, spatial- and time-dependent uncertainties; and (4) intelligent approaches that couple data-driven techniques with physical modelling. Reinforcement and protection technologies are subsequently reviewed, including conventional measures for rock/soil slope stabilization, as well as structural reinforcement, seepage control and ecological stabilization approaches specifically for soft rock slopes. Finally, this paper outlines future perspectives, including coupling multiphysics modelling with multi-source intelligent monitoring; advancing nature-based protection and durable protective materials; and integrating these into digital-twin platforms for dynamic reliability assessment and AI-assisted decision optimization in soft rock slope management. © The Author(s) 2026. Authors: Duc N.T.
Author full names: Duc, Nguyen Trung (58199623800)
Title: From mechanistic models to breeding digital twins: Predictive plant improvement for a changing climate
Affiliations: Vietnam National University of Agriculture, Hanoi, Viet Nam
Authors with affiliations: Duc N.T., Vietnam National University of Agriculture, Hanoi, Viet Nam
Abstract: Climate change is making historical phenotypes less reliable guides to future breeding environments, turning prediction into a central problem for plant science. Yet many predictive tools still end at model output, with limited connection to auditable breeding decisions. Here we frame predictive plant improvement as a breeding digital twin problem: a twin must specify a breeding referent, mutable state vector, counterfactual action space, utility function, and prospective audit. Using sweet corn as a stress test, we show how endosperm genetics, product-system quality, seed feasibility, genomic prediction, breeding simulation, and decision science can be organized into auditable breeding intelligence. Rather than replacing fields or breeders, the framework makes crossing, trial, selection, and release decisions more anticipatory under climate uncertainty. The prediction target is not a single phenotype but the joint consequence of breeding decisions for product quality, climate-conditioned resilience, seed feasibility, and program efficiency. © 2026 Elsevier Inc.

Abstract: This study presents an automated 3D scan-to-model framework for historic buildings using point cloud data. An enhanced PointNet++ architecture enables component-level semantic segmentation and progressive surface segmentation. Geometric fitting couples RANSAC with NURBS to preserve surface continuity and achieve high-fidelity modeling of complex timber components without template libraries. To ensure interpretability and reliability, an integrated accuracy–uncertainty scheme is introduced, applying residual statistics and Jacobian-based covariance propagation to quantify residual distributions between point clouds and fitted surfaces, as well as uncertainty in normal orientations. Experiments on a representative Tibetan historic timber structure demonstrate millimeter-level geometric accuracy and yield error maps and uncertainty indices. The framework delivers geometric fidelity and completeness of detail, and provides a unified basis for accuracy and reliability verification, thereby supporting HBIM integration, structural assessment, and future digital twin development for heritage conservation. Title: Physics-Embedded Hybrid Neural ODE With Digital Twin Residuals for Fault Diagnosis in Grid-Connected Photovoltaic Systems

Authors with affiliations: Mansouri M., Sultan Qaboos University, College of Engineering, Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, Muscat, 123, Oman
Abstract: Accurate and interpretable fault diagnosis in renewable energy systems remains challenging due to measurement noise, nonlinear operating conditions, model uncertainty, and the presence of interacting fault mechanisms. This paper proposes a Physics-Embedded Hybrid Neural Ordinary Differential Equation (PE-HANODE) framework augmented with Digital Twin (DT) residual information for robust diagnosis of multi-fault, non-Gaussian, and time-varying conditions in grid-connected photovoltaic (PV) systems. The main contribution of this work is not the introduction of individual new learning components, but the development of a unified diagnostic framework that integrates complementary physics-guided representations, lightweight Digital Twin residual reasoning, attention-guided feature weighting, and Neural ODE-based temporal modeling to address limitations of conventional data-driven PV fault diagnosis approaches. The proposed framework integrates three complementary components. First, physics-informed features derived from PV electrical characteristics and operating principles provide physically meaningful representations of system behavior rather than relying solely on data-driven feature extraction. Second, a lightweight DT model identified from healthy operating data generates residual signals that quantify deviations between expected nominal responses and measured system behavior, while the SDM is employed for physical consistency verification and parameter calibration rather than direct residual generation. Third, an attention-guided Neural ODE architecture exploits continuous latent-state evolution to capture temporal dependencies while prioritizing diagnostically relevant features. The DT residuals are fused with measured and physics-informed variables and incorporated into the Neural ODE learning process, enabling improved discrimination of subtle and overlapping fault signatures under noisy and incomplete sensing conditions. The attention mechanism provides feature-level interpretability by highlighting the relative importance of diagnostic variables and residual signals contributing to classification decisions, rather than performing direct physical root-cause identification. The effectiveness of the proposed approach is validated using both synthetic PV fault datasets for controlled proof-of-concept evaluation and experimental data obtained from an emulated laboratory-scale PV platform representing more realistic operating conditions. Additional robustness studies are conducted under Laplace and uniform noise perturbations to evaluate resilience against non-Gaussian measurement uncertainty. Comparative results demonstrate that the integration of physics-guided features, DT residual information, attention-based feature weighting, and continuous-time latent representation learning provides consistent diagnostic improvements compared with conventional machine learning and recurrent neural network baselines, including LSTM and GRU models. Ablation studies, statistical performance analysis, and computational complexity evaluations are further conducted to quantify the contribution of each framework component and assess the trade-off between diagnostic performance and computational requirements. Interpretability analyses based on attention-weight distributions and fault-confusion assessment provide insights into feature importance patterns within the learned diagnostic representation. The proposed PE-HANODE framework offers a physics-consistent and interpretable solution for intelligent fault diagnosis by unifying physics-informed feature construction, lightweight Digital Twin residual generation, and continuous-time deep learning within a single diagnostic architecture. The proposed framework demonstrates promising capability for real-time PV monitoring under evaluated laboratory conditions, while further utility-scale field validation remains necessary before large-scale industrial deployment.INDEX TERMS Physics-embedded neural ODE, digital twin, fault diagnosis, photovoltaic systems, attention mechanism, explainable artificial intelligence, continuous-time learning.  © 2013 IEEE.

Title: Digital Twins as the Implementation Layer of Precision Medicine in Pediatric Neurosurgery
Affiliations: Artificial Intelligence Research Center, JLK Inc., Seoul, South Korea
Authors with affiliations: Koh E.J., Artificial Intelligence Research Center, JLK Inc., Seoul, South Korea
Abstract: Pediatric neurosurgery increasingly utilizes precision medicine, but practitioners encounter challenges in translating complex data into individualized care. Digital twin (DT) bridges this gap by linking real-world data to a dynamic patient in-silico model, facilitating prediction and adaptive management as new data emerge. This narrative review explores the essential features of DTs, highlighting their relevance and associated risks in pediatric neurosurgery. The DT framework is structured around five components: the patient, a data connection, a patient-in-silico model, a clinician interface, and temporal synchronization. Foundational modeling approaches are summarized, spanning mechanistic simulations, artificial intelligence, and hybrid models that combine mechanistic structure with datadriven inference. Clinical translation is framed around uncertainty and calibration, along with interpretability and detection of distribution shifts. Potential applications are organized by concrete clinical questions in epilepsy surgery, pediatric neuro-oncology, cerebrovascular disease, hydrocephalus, and craniosynostosis. A translational pathway is outlined that progresses from decision-oriented prototypes and retrospective validation to prospective evaluation and interventional studies within learning health systems, supported by robust governance and auditable workflows. With meticulous validation and cautious deployment tailored to pediatric populations, DTs may enhance transparency, testability, and shared decision-making in precision pediatric neurosurgery. © 2026 The Korean Neurosurgical Society.

Title: Hybrid physics-based and data-driven digital twinning of a 6 MW offshore wind turbine
Affiliations: Dept. of Civil and Environmental Engineering, Tufts University, Medford, MA, United States; Dept. of Civil and Environmental Engineering, Northeastern University, Boston, MA, United States
Authors with affiliations: Bagirgan B., Dept. of Civil and Environmental Engineering, Tufts University, Medford, MA, United States; Tronci E.M., Dept. of Civil and Environmental Engineering, Tufts University, Medford, MA, United States, Dept. of Civil and Environmental Engineering, Northeastern University, Boston, MA, United States; Moaveni B., Dept. of Civil and Environmental Engineering, Tufts University, Medford, MA, United States; Hines E., Dept. of Civil and Environmental Engineering, Tufts University, Medford, MA, United States
Abstract: This study focuses on the development of a hybrid digital twin of a 6 MW offshore wind turbine (OWT), which integrated both physics-based and data-driven models with measurements. The primary objective is to model the complex dynamic behavior of an OWT at varying environmental and operational conditions. An initial finite element model of the turbine is created using design information and is calibrated to match the dynamic measurements by tuning the soil springs. The aerodynamic effects are then modeled by considering an additional spring at the hub height, serves as a physically interpretable single parameter used to represent aerodynamic stiffening effects, with its stiffness iteratively updated to represent turbine's modal parameters extracted from measured acceleration data. A data-driven model is developed to correlate hub-height spring stiffness with varying operating conditions, based on stiffness values obtained from the updated finite element model, enabling prediction of turbine's dynamic response across different scenarios. This model is implemented using a long short-term memory (LSTM) architecture, and its predictive uncertainty is quantified through a Monte Carlo dropout strategy. The final optimal prediction of stiffness at the hub is used to correct the initial model and reliably predict the dynamic response of the turbine. The novelty of this work lies in the hybrid integration of system identification–based finite element updating with uncertainty-aware machine learning to predict physically interpretable model parameters. The results indicate that the LSTM model is capable of representing the aerodynamic stiffening effect on the OWT and significantly improves the dynamic response predictions. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Title: A Hybrid Automaton-Based Vehicle Digital Twin for Verifiable Pedestrian Protection
Affiliations: University of Bologna, Bologna, 40126, Italy; Suor Orsola Benincasa, Centro Scienza Nuova, Naples, 80135, Italy
Authors with affiliations: Bacchiani L., University of Bologna, Bologna, 40126, Italy; Bedei A., University of Bologna, Bologna, 40126, Italy; Kaya O., University of Bologna, Bologna, 40126, Italy; Presta R., Suor Orsola Benincasa, Centro Scienza Nuova, Naples, 80135, Italy; Bravetti M., University of Bologna, Bologna, 40126, Italy; Girau R., University of Bologna, Bologna, 40126, Italy
Abstract: Autonomous vehicles must make reliable safety decisions despite perception noise and tight timing constraints. This work presents a Vehicle Digital Twin (VDT) architecture that incorporates a formally verified hybrid automaton as its supervisory controller. The automaton specifies discrete safety modes, continuous timing variables, and perception-driven transitions, and is verified offline using SMT-based LTL model checking to ensure determinism, freedom from deadlock, and bounded reaction time. At runtime, buffered perception inputs and staleness checks are used to trigger only those transitions consistent with the verified model, maintaining robustness to noisy or transient detections. We instantiate the approach for pedestrian-protection and evaluate it on standardized Euro NCAP scenarios within CARLA. The system consistently produces stable and interpretable braking decisions and maintains reaction times within the verified bounds, including under perception uncertainty. These results indicate that integrating a verified hybrid automaton directly into the VDT's operational loop is a practical route toward runtime-assured safety supervision in perception-driven vehicle systems.  © 2026 The Authors.

Title: AI-Powered Digital Twins for Building Energy Management: Modeling Frameworks, Validation and Uncertainty Quantification, Smart Grid Integration, and Deployment Roadmap
Affiliations: AGH University of Krakow, Faculty of Metals Engineering and Industrial Computer Science, al. Mickiewicza 30, Krakow, 30-059, Poland
Authors with affiliations: Łach Ł., AGH University of Krakow, Faculty of Metals Engineering and Industrial Computer Science, al. Mickiewicza 30, Krakow, 30-059, Poland
Abstract: The global buildings and construction sector remains a dominant contributor to anthropogenic climate change, and deep decarbonization has positioned digital twin technology as a transformative pathway for intelligent building energy management. Despite considerable research momentum, the field lacks a coherent synthesis mapping AI capabilities onto the full digital twin lifecycle—from sensor-driven calibration through real-world deployment to district-scale operation. This review addresses this gap through six objectives: analyzing AI-enhanced modeling approaches for building digital twins; examining data infrastructure and interoperability requirements; evaluating validation, calibration, and uncertainty quantification practices; synthesizing real-world implementation evidence across diverse building typologies; assessing integration with renewable energy systems and smart grids; and identifying challenges, research gaps, and a strategic deployment roadmap. Physics-based, data-driven, and hybrid modeling strategies occupy distinct and complementary roles. Physics-informed surrogate models preserve thermodynamic interpretability while reducing computational overhead; deep learning architectures—including recurrent networks and reinforcement learning agents—deliver adaptive control; and federated learning frameworks enable privacy-preserving optimization across distributed building portfolios. Rigorous multi-metric validation aligned with established calibration standards proves essential for trustworthy deployment, while Bayesian and ensemble-based uncertainty quantification methods emerge as indispensable components of operationally credible digital twins. Evidence from real-world deployments in residential, commercial, healthcare, and industrial facilities confirms that AI-powered digital twins consistently deliver substantial energy savings and measurable improvements in occupant comfort. Scaling to district and urban levels introduces challenges in data governance, computational architecture, and multi-stakeholder coordination, yet federated digital twin frameworks are beginning to demonstrate viable pathways. The paper concludes with a decade-long strategic roadmap spanning technological maturation, market development, regulatory alignment, and decarbonization impact—positioning AI-enhanced digital twins not as incremental optimization tools, but as the foundational infrastructure for the coordinated transformation of the global building stock. © 2026 by the author.

Title: Smart manufacturing of nanocomposites: Digital twins, process engineering, and translational industrialization
Affiliations: Saveetha College of Pharmacy, Saveetha Institute of Medical and Technical Sciences, Chennai, 602105, India
Authors with affiliations: Eluri K., Saveetha College of Pharmacy, Saveetha Institute of Medical and Technical Sciences, Chennai, 602105, India; Krishnakumar G., Saveetha College of Pharmacy, Saveetha Institute of Medical and Technical Sciences, Chennai, 602105, India; Elumalai K., Saveetha College of Pharmacy, Saveetha Institute of Medical and Technical Sciences, Chennai, 602105, India
Abstract: Carbon nanotubes, graphene derivatives, MXenes, metal oxides, nanocellulose, and hybrid nanofillers exhibit outstanding reinforcement properties, such as mechanical strength, electrical conductivity, thermal transport, barrier properties, and multifunctionality, in thermoplastic and thermosetting matrices. However, the ability to produce these materials on an industrial scale is still hindered by many challenges, such as the variability of the raw materials, degradation of the properties when the materials agglomerate, high-throughput processing challenges due to the instability of the dispersion, high energy consumption of dispersion processes, limited window of manufacturability, quality control requirements, recycling limitations, and uncertainty regarding regulatory requirements. This review introduces a manufacturing framework to translate nanocomposites on the basis of a process-driven and systems engineering approach rather than just a material design perspective. This review addresses the processing methods that can be used on a large scale, such as melt compounding, reactive extrusion, solution-assisted processing, additively manufactured components, and roll-to-roll fabrication, and explores the dispersion behaviour, interphase evolution, orientation of the fillers, percolation behaviour, formation of defects, and functional reproducibility under different processing conditions. Special emphasis is placed on the coupled relationships between transport phenomena, rheological evolution, and multiscale structural organization, which are responsible for manufacturing scalability and deployment readiness. Emerging Industry 4.0 technologies, such as process analytical technologies (PATs), inline metrology, machine learning, digital twins, and autonomous process control, have been tested for their potential to predict and control important manufacturing metrics, such as dispersion quality, rheological behavior, filler-network formation, defect occurrence, and process consistency, through real-time data integration and adaptive feedback systems. The review also incorporates technoeconomic analysis, life cycle assessment, circular manufacturing approaches, and regulatory aspects to assess industrial feasibility for various application fields, such as aerospace, electronics, energy, biomedical, and multifunctional coatings. Finally, future directions include designs for manufacturing compatible nanomaterials, predictive multiscale modelling, certification structures enabled by digital, autonomous production systems, and sustainable industrial ecosystems. This review offers a complete overview of the challenges of scaling up the industrialization of advanced nanocomposite materials to be reproducible and economically viable while maintaining nanomaterial engineering, manufacturing science, digitalization, and lifecycle sustainability. © 2026 The Authors

Abstract: Efficient billet heating is a critical economic and environmental challenge in wire-rod steel rolling. This work presents an artificial-intelligence (AI) framework to support energy-consumption reduction in an industrial induction furnace by combining a calibrated finite-element (FE) digital twin, a deep-learning (DL) surrogate, and a deep reinforcement learning agent. The FE model, calibrated with real production data from Global Steel Wire (Spain), reproduces the outlet-temperature trends of the resulfurized billet family with RMSE < 5 °C and Pearson correlation > 0.95. To enable fast surrogate-based optimization, a convolutional-recurrent surrogate was trained using real plant time series as inputs and FE-simulated outlet-temperature profiles for those same real billets as target outputs, achieving RMSE values of 5.7 °C on the training billets and 9.85 °C on the test billets, both within the uncertainty range of the outlet pyrometer. This surrogate was then embedded as the environment of a Deep Q-Learning (DQL) framework that searches for lower-energy heating schedules under practical operational constraints and the prescribed outlet-temperature similarity criterion. Across the evaluated resulfurized billets, the learned policy reduced surrogate-predicted energy consumption in every case while keeping the predicted exit-temperature profiles close to the prescribed 5 °C RMSE similarity threshold to the target profile. In representative cases, the surrogate-predicted savings reached 24% and 27%. These results indicate the potential of reinforcement learning as a supervisory decision-support layer for induction-furnace energy optimization when coupled with a physically grounded and computationally efficient digital environment. However, FE re-evaluation and plant-level validation of the optimized schedules are required before industrial deployment. © The Author(s) 2026.

Abstract: In this paper, we study a social-aware resource allocation problem for multi-modal virtual-physical interaction systems. In the considered system, multiple users interact with each other in a shared virtual model (e.g., a Metaverse or digital twin) hosted on an edge server deployed at a base station. This social interaction creates complex dynamics, leading to highly uncertain and time-varying user behaviors and requirements for multi-modal feedback (including visual and haptic). This social-driven uncertainty poses a significant challenge for resource allocation at the edge server. Our objective is to maximize the long-term quality of experience (QoE) of all users by jointly optimizing the edge server's bandwidth and CPU frequency allocations, and multi-modal feedback configurations. To tackle this challenge, leveraging the strong generalization capability of continual reinforcement learning (CRL), we propose a novel CRL-based approach, termed CRL-based social-aware resource allocation approach (CRL-SARA). Simulation results show the effectiveness of CRL-SARA and demonstrate its superiority over the existing schemes. © 2026 IEEE.

Abstract: The delivery of telesurgical services to rural areas is hindered by unpredictable connectivity and limited infrastructure. While Low Earth Orbit (LEO) satellites offer promising low-latency coverage, their performance is vulnerable to visibility loss, handoffs, and link failures. To address this, we propose a Satellite Robotic Telesurgery Digital Twin (SRTDT) framework that integrates causal forecasting with a proxy-surgeon failover mechanism to ensure surgical continuity under network disruptions. Using twelve hours of simulated LEO data, we demonstrate: (i) a multitask deep learning model that predicts satellite visibility and failure types with 88% accuracy; (ii) a causal analysis linking orbital dynamics, such as: elevation, slant range, and path loss to the network KPIs including latency, jitter, throughput and packet loss; and (iii) an interpretable XGBoost+SHAP model that identifies elevation as a dominant driver of end to end delay, supported by Granger causality tests. In a simulated two-hour surgical procedure, our proactive failover mechanism recovered 57% of the execution time lost to network outages, enabling either a safe resumption or a controlled termination of the operation. These results underscore the potential of integrating causal forecasting with autonomous failover to mitigate the risks of satellite dependent telesurgery in remote settings. © 2026 IEEE.

Abstract: High-fidelity finite element analysis (FEA) of unbonded flexible pipes is computationally prohibitive—approximately 60min per simulation—rendering Monte Carlo reliability analysis and real-time digital twin operation infeasible. Existing POD-based surrogates—Kriging, PCE, and ANN regressors—address at most four continuous load parameters and assume smooth, unimodal parameter-to-response manifolds, leaving the eight-dimensional, six-category, contact-nonlinear load space of flexible pipes unresolved. This paper presents FEM–POD–PIT (contact-resolved FEM, Proper Orthogonal Decomposition, and a Physics-Informed Transformer) for quasi-static response, with two scientific contributions: the first, to the authors’ knowledge, systematic quantification of rank heterogeneity in helically periodic offshore structures, and a Riemannian-derived Helical Positional Encoding (HPE) whose ablation-verified contribution is ΔR2=+0.542[jls-end-space/]. A contact-resolved ABAQUS model (331,492 nodes; 994,476 DOF) provided 4500 snapshots across six load categories. A 30-mode POD basis achieves (Formula presented) compression (R2=1.0000[jls-end-space/]); rank heterogeneity is identified: r∗=2 for tension–pressure versus r∗=18 for torsion, attributed to multi-harmonic opposing-helix fields. The PIT ((Formula presented) parameters), trained on 54 cases (2700 snapshots), achieves R2=0.9910 on the held-out synthetic test set (ΔR2=+0.468 over an MLP baseline; per-type variation <0.001[jls-end-space/]); torsion exhibits elevated error (Ru2=0.861[jls-end-space/]) on real ABAQUS data owing to synthetic-to-real domain mismatch. Inference requires (Formula presented), enabling 105 Monte Carlo evaluations in (Formula presented) versus 11.4 years by direct FEA—a 6.5×105[jls-end-space/]-fold speedup. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Abstract: Geometric fidelity is a fundamental prerequisite for reliable cognitive digital twins (CDTs). An inaccurate or incomplete as-is geometric foundation leads to model uncertainty, thereby undermining CDT reasoning and maintenance decisions. However, point cloud data (PCD) acquired through laser scanning is inevitably subject to occlusions caused by structural obstructions, sensor limitations, and complex mechanical, electrical, and plumbing (MEP) configurations, introducing geometric uncertainty that undermines the trustworthiness of as-is digital twin representations. Existing methods fail to address the high-precision full spectrum of occlusion scenarios in real-world Scan-to/versus-BIM (Building Information Modeling/Model) workflows, particularly for border truncations and irregular non-Manhattan geometries. This paper proposes a method that systematically reduces geometric uncertainty in CDT construction through three stages. First, a gap classification scheme categorizes incomplete point clusters by occlusion severity and object class, enabling targeted treatment of each scenario for both Manhattan and non-Manhattan geometries. The completed clusters are then tessellated into high-resolution meshes and converted into Industry Foundation Classes (IFC) models through a new purpose-designed data structure that embeds laser-scan timestamps and as-designed global identifier links. Together, these stages form a closed-loop geometric DT updating system that continuously reflects the as-is physical state of the building, directly reducing the geometric uncertainty that would otherwise propagate into CDT-based maintenance reasoning and risk assessment. The method is validated on various real-world datasets. The performance is evaluated with ground truth (GT) and Chamfer distance (CD), with results benchmarked against Level of Accuracy (LOA) requirements to confirm practical ability. The resulting timestamped IFC models provide a geometrically reliable foundation for CDT-based predictive maintenance and facility risk assessment. Copyright © 2026 by ASME.

Title: Foundation Models Meet Musculoskeletal Digital Twins: Uncertainty-Aware Early Detection of Subclinical Cartilage Damage via Cross-Modal Transfer Learning
Source title: IEEE Journal of Biomedical and Health Informatics
Affiliations: Xi'an Jiaotong University, Honghui Hospital, Comprehensive Department, Bone Trauma Hospital, Shaanxi, Xi'an, 710054, China
Authors with affiliations: Feng H., Xi'an Jiaotong University, Honghui Hospital, Comprehensive Department, Bone Trauma Hospital, Shaanxi, Xi'an, 710054, China; Peng D., Xi'an Jiaotong University, Honghui Hospital, Comprehensive Department, Bone Trauma Hospital, Shaanxi, Xi'an, 710054, China
Abstract: Detecting early cartilage degeneration on MRI remains challenging because early compositional changes produce only subtle signal variations easily confounded with normal anatomical and acquisition variability. We pro pose CartiDT, a cross-modal transfer learning framework that couples vision foundation models with musculoskeletal digital twin representations for preclinical cartilage dam age detection. CartiDT comprises three modules: (1) a parameter-efficient adaptation module that transfers frozen vision transformer features to three-dimensional double echo steady-state knee MRI via depth-wise Low-RankAdap tation and depth-axis positional interpolation; (2) a graph neural network encoder whose biomechanically derived adjacency captures inter-compartment dependencies within a lightweight digital twin; and (3) an evidential deep learning head that decomposes predictive uncertainty into aleatoric and epistemic components, enabling the model to abstain on unreliable predictions. Evaluated on the Osteoarthri tis Initiative longitudinal dataset (4,796 subjects), CartiDT achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.861 (±0.003) for preclinical damage detection and a Dice similarity coefficient of 0.879 (±0.002) for six-compartment segmentation, surpassing the strongest baselines by 3.8 and 1.2 percentage points, respectively. Selective prediction based on uncertainty awareness eliminated 29.6% of false positives when compared to the most powerful uncertainty-aware baseline (the equivalent of a five-member deep ensemble) with a 15% referral bar, with only one forward pass (3.2 s/volume, compared to 16 s/volume); the increased calibration and the increase in speed are positive and separate benefits. Patellar cartilage remained the most difficult compartment (Dice 0.814, detection AUROC 0.806), and the digital twin module added a modest 18% wall-clock overhead versus segmentation alone. These results demonstrate that integrating foundation model representations with structured anatomical priors enhances early cartilage damage detection, while thin-cartilage regions and computational cost remain open challenges. © 2013 IEEE.
